report.name: Blocking Sessions
report.description: Point-in-time blocking diagnosis: who blocks whom (full chains), the blockers' identity, transactions and SQL, every lock held or requested with its type decoded, and the objects and rows being fought over. Run it WHILE the blocking is happening — an empty result means no blocking at collection time.
report.analysis_instructions:
IDIOMA: escreva TODO o relatório em português (pt-BR). Não traduza jargão técnico consagrado (lock, enqueue, commit, rollback, blocking session, ITL etc.).

The line above defines the report's OUTPUT LANGUAGE. EVERYTHING in the report is written in that language: prose, table headers, fixed labels and EVERY section title. The English titles and labels in this specification are meant to be TRANSLATED into the output language, never copied verbatim. Only untranslatable technical jargon stays in English. Numbering, order and meaning never change.

This is a POINT-IN-TIME blocking diagnosis: the data is a snapshot of the moment the report ran. If the collection shows NO blocking (the summary query returned no rows), say exactly that in section 1 — the database had no session blocking at collection time — keep sections 2-5 to one line each stating there is nothing to report, and skip recommendations that assume a problem. Never invent blocking that the data does not show. Each query's description starts with a tag [1]-[5] naming the section where it must be handled.

FORMAT (Markdown): each section title as a level-2 heading ("## 1. …"), title text always in the output language. Blank line between titles, paragraphs, lists and tables. Tables ALWAYS as complete Markdown — header row, |---|---| separator and one line per record.

1. Blocking Snapshot (Portuguese title: Panorama do Bloqueio) — the situation in numbers: how many blockers, how many blocked sessions IN TOTAL (all lock types together, not just the dominant event's count), longest wait, the dominant wait events. One short paragraph a manager could read.

2. Blocking Chains (Portuguese title: Cadeias de Bloqueio) — read the tree: the root blocker(s) at depth 1, who waits under them, chain depths. Point out the root session(s) by inst:sid explicitly.

3. Blockers in Detail (Portuguese title: Bloqueadores em Detalhe) — for EACH root blocker: who it is (user, machine, program, module), its state (an INACTIVE blocker with an old transaction = idle-in-transaction, name it as such), how old its transaction is and how much undo it holds, and what SQL it runs now (CURRENT) or ran last (PREVIOUS). The PREVIOUS statement of an idle blocker usually names the statement that took the lock.

4. Blocked Sessions (Portuguese title: Sessões Bloqueadas) — who is stuck: count, identities, how long, and WHAT they are trying to run. Group victims by blocker when there are many.

5. Lock Source Analysis (Portuguese title: Análise da Origem do Lock) — the heart of this report. For EACH lock type present in the lock map, explain its mechanism and the likely root cause IN THIS DATA, tying event + lock type + objects + rows together. Use this knowledge, only where the data shows the type: TX with "row lock contention" = an uncommitted change to the SAME row (name the object and ROWID when the contended-rows query shows them); TX requested in share (S) mode = ITL shortage or unique/PK collision (a TX request in EXCLUSIVE (X) mode, as the lock map shows here, is plain row contention — never attribute it to ITL); TM = table-level DML lock — the classic cause is an UNINDEXED FOREIGN KEY on a child table, or LOCK TABLE/DDL mixing with DML (read the HELD mode in the lock map: an unindexed-FK TM lock is taken in share / row-X (SX) mode, while a TM held in EXCLUSIVE (X) mode points to LOCK TABLE/DDL, not an FK); UL = the application's own DBMS_LOCK usage (an application design fact, not a database fault); SQ = sequence cache contention (small or NOCACHE sequence); HW = concurrent inserts growing the same segment (LOB/freelist pressure); RO/CF/CI/PS/ST/TS = system-side coordination, usually a symptom of another operation (name it). Never present a mechanism for a lock type the data does not show.

6. Recommended Actions (Portuguese title: Ações Recomendadas) — two lists. IMMEDIATE: what to do about the current blockage — commit/rollback from the blocking application if reachable; otherwise ONE separate kill statement per root blocker (one line each, never merged) with its exact identifiers, clearly labeled as a command for the DBA to review and run manually — this tool is read-only and never executes it: ALTER SYSTEM KILL SESSION 'sid,serial#,@inst_id' IMMEDIATE; Before ANY kill recommendation, state that session's ROLLBACK COST from the transaction query (uncommitted undo in MB / blocks / records): the kill forces Oracle to undo exactly that much and the locks stay held during that recovery, so a large undo_mb means the kill is neither instant nor free — when it is large, prefer a clean COMMIT/ROLLBACK from the application and recommend the kill only with the cost stated so the DBA accepts it knowingly. A blocker with NO transaction row (LOCK TABLE/DDL/DBMS_LOCK) has nothing to roll back — a kill there is cheap. STRUCTURAL: what prevents recurrence, tied to the lock source found (index the named FK, commit discipline in the named module, sequence CACHE increase, ITL/INITRANS on the named table, review of the DBMS_LOCK design...).

7. Queries not collected (Portuguese title: Consultas não coletadas) — list each "NOT COLLECTED" query with its ORA error and likely cause. If none: say in one line, in the output language, that all queries were collected successfully.

Final rules: use exclusively this run's results; cite real inst:sid, users, objects and waits from the data; recommend nothing without evidence; a kill recommendation must name ONLY the ROOT blockers — a root is a session that is NOT itself blocked (depth 1 in the tree, blocking_session NULL). A session that BOTH blocks AND is blocked (a middle of the chain, e.g. a depth-2+ node that still has sessions under it) is NOT a kill target: killing its own root frees it by cascade and, being active, it usually finishes on its own — never put a middle-of-chain session in the kill list; escalating to it is a separate later step only if it still blocks after the root is gone; professional, direct, didactic tone.

sqls.name: Blocker — Summary
sqls.description: [1] One row per blocker: how many sessions it blocks and for how long (min/max wait). Empty = NO blocking at collection time — say so plainly and keep the whole report short.
sqls.sql:
SELECT w.blocking_instance inst_id,
       w.blocking_session sid,
       b.serial#,
       COUNT(*) sessions_blocked,
       COUNT(DISTINCT w.event) distinct_wait_events,
       MIN(w.seconds_in_wait) min_wait_seconds,
       MAX(w.seconds_in_wait) max_wait_seconds
  FROM gv$session w
  JOIN gv$session b
    ON b.inst_id = w.blocking_instance
   AND b.sid = w.blocking_session
 WHERE w.blocking_session IS NOT NULL
 GROUP BY w.blocking_instance, w.blocking_session, b.serial#
 ORDER BY sessions_blocked DESC;

sqls.name: Blocker — Session Detail
sqls.description: [3] Full identity of every blocker: who (user/OS user/machine/program/module), state (ACTIVE vs INACTIVE — an INACTIVE blocker holding locks is the classic idle-in-transaction), what it waits on itself, its current and previous SQL ids, last_call_et (seconds since its last activity) and logon time.
sqls.sql:
SELECT s.inst_id,
       s.sid,
       s.serial#,
       s.username,
       s.osuser,
       s.machine,
       s.program,
       s.module,
       s.action,
       s.status,
       s.state,
       s.event current_event,
       s.seconds_in_wait,
       s.last_call_et seconds_since_last_call,
       s.sql_id current_sql_id,
       s.prev_sql_id,
       TO_CHAR(s.logon_time, 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS') logon_time
  FROM gv$session s
 WHERE (s.inst_id, s.sid) IN (SELECT w.blocking_instance, w.blocking_session
                                FROM gv$session w
                               WHERE w.blocking_session IS NOT NULL)
 ORDER BY s.inst_id, s.sid;

sqls.name: Blocker — Open Transaction
sqls.description: [3] The open transaction behind each blocker, ordered by rollback cost. undo_blocks / undo_records / UNDO_MB are how much uncommitted work it holds — and also its ROLLBACK COST: killing this session forces Oracle to undo exactly this much, slow and I/O-heavy for a large transaction, with the locks held during recovery. An old transaction with tiny undo = someone forgot to commit; a large undo_mb = a real batch whose kill is not free. No row for a blocker = it holds locks WITHOUT an active transaction (LOCK TABLE/DDL, library cache, DBMS_LOCK) — nothing to roll back, so a kill there is cheap.
sqls.sql:
SELECT s.inst_id,
       s.sid,
       s.serial#,
       s.username,
       t.status tx_status,
       t.start_time tx_start_time,
       ROUND((SYSDATE - TO_DATE(t.start_time, 'MM/DD/RR HH24:MI:SS')) * 86400)
         tx_age_seconds,
       t.used_ublk undo_blocks,
       t.used_urec undo_records,
       ROUND(t.used_ublk *
             (SELECT TO_NUMBER(value) FROM v$parameter WHERE name = 'db_block_size')
             / 1048576, 1) undo_mb,
       (SELECT r.segment_name FROM dba_rollback_segs r WHERE r.segment_id = t.xidusn) undo_segment,
       t.log_io,
       t.phy_io
  FROM gv$transaction t
  JOIN gv$session s
    ON s.saddr = t.ses_addr
   AND s.inst_id = t.inst_id
 WHERE (s.inst_id, s.sid) IN (SELECT w.blocking_instance, w.blocking_session
                                FROM gv$session w
                               WHERE w.blocking_session IS NOT NULL)
 ORDER BY undo_mb DESC NULLS LAST;

sqls.name: Blocker — Current & Previous SQL
sqls.description: [3] What each blocker is running now (CURRENT; empty when it sits idle) and the last thing it ran (PREVIOUS) — for an idle-in-transaction blocker, PREVIOUS usually names the statement that took the lock.
sqls.sql:
SELECT s.inst_id,
       s.sid,
       s.serial#,
       'CURRENT' which_sql,
       q.sql_id,
       q.sql_text
  FROM gv$session s
  JOIN gv$sql q
    ON q.inst_id = s.inst_id
   AND q.sql_id = s.sql_id
   AND q.child_number = 0
 WHERE (s.inst_id, s.sid) IN (SELECT w.blocking_instance, w.blocking_session
                                FROM gv$session w
                               WHERE w.blocking_session IS NOT NULL)
UNION ALL
SELECT s.inst_id,
       s.sid,
       s.serial#,
       'PREVIOUS' which_sql,
       q.sql_id,
       q.sql_text
  FROM gv$session s
  JOIN gv$sql q
    ON q.inst_id = s.inst_id
   AND q.sql_id = s.prev_sql_id
   AND q.child_number = 0
 WHERE (s.inst_id, s.sid) IN (SELECT w.blocking_instance, w.blocking_session
                                FROM gv$session w
                               WHERE w.blocking_session IS NOT NULL)
 ORDER BY 1, 2, 4;

sqls.name: Chain — Blocking Tree (blocker → blocked)
sqls.description: [2] The wait chains, root blocker first (depth 1); each deeper row waits on the row above it. A depth-1 session blocking many = the root cause; chains more than 2 deep mean blocked sessions are themselves blocking.
sqls.sql:
SELECT CASE WHEN LEVEL = 1
            THEN s.inst_id || ':' || s.sid
            ELSE LPAD('-', (LEVEL - 1) * 4, '-') || '> '
                 || s.inst_id || ':' || s.sid
       END session_ref,
       LEVEL depth,
       s.serial#,
       s.username,
       s.status,
       s.event,
       s.seconds_in_wait,
       s.sql_id,
       s.module,
       s.machine
  FROM gv$session s
 START WITH s.blocking_session IS NULL
        AND (s.inst_id, s.sid) IN (SELECT w.blocking_instance, w.blocking_session
                                FROM gv$session w
                               WHERE w.blocking_session IS NOT NULL)
CONNECT BY s.blocking_session = PRIOR s.sid
       AND s.blocking_instance = PRIOR s.inst_id
 ORDER SIBLINGS BY s.seconds_in_wait DESC;

sqls.name: Blocker ↔ Blocked — Pairs (lock type, object, row)
sqls.description: [2] One row per blocker↔blocked pair, side by side: the lock TYPE from v$lock_type (Transaction/DML/User-defined/...), both sessions' events, the object and the exact contended ROWID. Complements the tree (hierarchy) with a flat pairing; its lock type and object also feed section 5. Non-row waits (TM/UL) still appear here, just without an object/row.
sqls.sql:
SELECT s1.inst_id || ':' || s1.sid || ',' || s1.serial# blocking_session,
       s2.inst_id || ':' || s2.sid || ',' || s2.serial# blocked_session,
       lt.name lock_type,
       s1.event blocking_event,
       s2.event blocked_event,
       CASE WHEN do.object_name IS NOT NULL
            THEN do.owner || '.' || do.object_name END object,
       CASE WHEN do.data_object_id IS NOT NULL AND s2.row_wait_obj# > 0
            THEN DBMS_ROWID.ROWID_CREATE(1, do.data_object_id, s2.row_wait_file#,
                                         s2.row_wait_block#, s2.row_wait_row#)
       END row_id
  FROM gv$lock l1
  JOIN gv$session s1 ON s1.inst_id = l1.inst_id AND s1.sid = l1.sid
  JOIN gv$lock l2 ON l2.id1 = l1.id1 AND l2.id2 = l1.id2
                 AND l2.type = l1.type AND l2.request > 0
  JOIN gv$session s2 ON s2.inst_id = l2.inst_id AND s2.sid = l2.sid
  LEFT JOIN (SELECT type, MAX(name) name FROM gv$lock_type GROUP BY type) lt
    ON lt.type = l1.type
  LEFT JOIN dba_objects do ON do.object_id = s2.row_wait_obj#
 WHERE l1.block > 0
 ORDER BY s1.inst_id, s1.sid, s2.sid;

sqls.name: Lock Map — held by blocker vs requested by blocked
sqls.description: [5] Every lock held that blocks someone (BLOCKS_OTHERS=1) or requested and not granted (MODE_REQUESTED <> none), with the lock TYPE decoded — the core evidence for the lock-source analysis. TX+row events = row contention; TM = table/FK; UL = the application's own DBMS_LOCK; HW = segment growth; SQ = sequence; TX requested in share (S) mode = ITL or same-row primary-key/unique wait.
sqls.sql:
SELECT l.inst_id,
       l.sid,
       s.serial#,
       s.username,
       l.type lock_type,
       CASE l.type
         WHEN 'TX' THEN 'Transaction (row lock / ITL / undo)'
         WHEN 'TM' THEN 'DML enqueue (table level)'
         WHEN 'UL' THEN 'User lock (DBMS_LOCK)'
         WHEN 'HW' THEN 'High-water mark (segment growth)'
         WHEN 'SQ' THEN 'Sequence cache'
         WHEN 'ST' THEN 'Space transaction'
         WHEN 'TS' THEN 'Temporary segment'
         WHEN 'RO' THEN 'Reusable object (cache flush)'
         WHEN 'CF' THEN 'Control file'
         WHEN 'JI' THEN 'Materialized view refresh'
         WHEN 'CI' THEN 'Cross-instance call'
         WHEN 'PS' THEN 'Parallel execution slave'
         WHEN 'DX' THEN 'Distributed transaction'
         WHEN 'AE' THEN 'Edition in use'
         ELSE 'Other/system enqueue'
       END lock_type_meaning,
       DECODE(l.lmode, 0, 'none', 1, 'null', 2, 'row-S (SS)',
              3, 'row-X (SX)', 4, 'share (S)', 5, 'S/row-X (SSX)',
              6, 'exclusive (X)', TO_CHAR(l.lmode)) mode_held,
       DECODE(l.request, 0, 'none', 1, 'null', 2, 'row-S (SS)',
              3, 'row-X (SX)', 4, 'share (S)', 5, 'S/row-X (SSX)',
              6, 'exclusive (X)', TO_CHAR(l.request)) mode_requested,
       l.id1,
       l.id2,
       l.ctime seconds_in_mode,
       l.block blocks_others
  FROM gv$lock l
  JOIN gv$session s
    ON s.inst_id = l.inst_id
   AND s.sid = l.sid
 WHERE l.block > 0
    OR l.request > 0
 ORDER BY l.type, l.id1, l.id2, l.request DESC;

sqls.name: Lock — Locked Objects (both sessions)
sqls.description: [5] The objects under DML locks and by whom, with the mode decoded — names WHAT is being fought over at object level.
sqls.sql:
SELECT lo.inst_id,
       lo.session_id sid,
       s.serial#,
       lo.oracle_username,
       o.owner,
       o.object_name,
       o.object_type,
       DECODE(lo.locked_mode, 0, 'none', 1, 'null', 2, 'row-S (SS)',
              3, 'row-X (SX)', 4, 'share (S)', 5, 'S/row-X (SSX)',
              6, 'exclusive (X)', TO_CHAR(lo.locked_mode)) locked_mode,
       lo.os_user_name,
       lo.process
  FROM gv$locked_object lo
  JOIN dba_objects o
    ON o.object_id = lo.object_id
  LEFT JOIN gv$session s
    ON s.inst_id = lo.inst_id
   AND s.sid = lo.session_id
 ORDER BY o.owner, o.object_name, lo.inst_id, lo.session_id;

sqls.name: Blocked — Wait Events
sqls.description: [1] What the blocked sessions are waiting ON — the event NAME points at the lock source (enq: TX - row lock contention = uncommitted change to the same row; enq: TM = table-level, often an unindexed FK; enq: TX - allocate ITL entry = ITL shortage; library cache lock = DDL vs SQL; row cache lock = dictionary, often sequences). The blocked_sessions column lists the inst:sid of every waiter on that event.
sqls.sql:
SELECT w.event,
       COUNT(*) sessions_waiting,
       MIN(w.seconds_in_wait) min_wait_seconds,
       MAX(w.seconds_in_wait) max_wait_seconds,
       LISTAGG(w.inst_id || ':' || w.sid, ', ' ON OVERFLOW TRUNCATE)
         WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY w.inst_id, w.sid) blocked_sessions
  FROM gv$session w
 WHERE w.blocking_session IS NOT NULL
 GROUP BY w.event
 ORDER BY sessions_waiting DESC;

sqls.name: Blocked — Session Detail
sqls.description: [4] Every blocked session (the victims): identity, the event and how long it has waited, what it is trying to run, and which session blocks it.
sqls.sql:
SELECT w.inst_id,
       w.sid,
       w.serial#,
       w.username,
       w.osuser,
       w.machine,
       w.program,
       w.module,
       w.event,
       w.seconds_in_wait,
       w.sql_id,
       w.blocking_instance || ':' || w.blocking_session blocked_by
  FROM gv$session w
 WHERE w.blocking_session IS NOT NULL
 ORDER BY w.seconds_in_wait DESC;

sqls.name: Blocked — SQL Being Attempted
sqls.description: [4] The statement each victim is trying to execute — names the application action that is stuck.
sqls.sql:
SELECT w.inst_id,
       w.sid,
       w.serial#,
       w.sql_id,
       q.sql_text
  FROM gv$session w
  JOIN gv$sql q
    ON q.inst_id = w.inst_id
   AND q.sql_id = w.sql_id
   AND q.child_number = 0
 WHERE w.blocking_session IS NOT NULL
 ORDER BY w.inst_id, w.sid;

sqls.name: Blocked — Contended Row
sqls.description: [5] Down to the ROW: the object and, when Oracle exposes it, the exact ROWID each victim is stuck on — the strongest evidence for row-level (TX) contention. Empty object columns = the wait is not row-positioned (e.g. library cache, DBMS_LOCK).
sqls.sql:
SELECT w.inst_id,
       w.sid,
       w.serial#,
       w.event,
       o.owner,
       o.object_name,
       o.object_type,
       w.row_wait_file# file_id,
       w.row_wait_block# block_id,
       w.row_wait_row# row_num,
       CASE
         WHEN o.data_object_id IS NOT NULL AND w.row_wait_obj# > 0
         THEN DBMS_ROWID.ROWID_CREATE(1, o.data_object_id, w.row_wait_file#,
                                      w.row_wait_block#, w.row_wait_row#)
       END row_id
  FROM gv$session w
  LEFT JOIN dba_objects o
    ON o.object_id = w.row_wait_obj#
 WHERE w.blocking_session IS NOT NULL
 ORDER BY o.owner, o.object_name, w.inst_id, w.sid;
